entries.threat: An attacker who influences a FunctionCall field type, directly or through tool or model output, runs arbitrary Python in the Agno process.
entries.conditions: Agno before 2.3.24 with FunctionCall inputs that user, tool or model content can influence.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to Agno 2.3.24 or later; until then keep untrusted input away from the field_type parameter.

entries.title: Early-exit LLMs: shallow exits resist GCG-style adversarial suffixes better than deep exits
entries.summary: Early exit lets a model produce output from an intermediate layer to save compute. This workshop paper tests jailbreaks that append a crafted suffix (extra text added to the prompt) at each exit depth, and finds that shallow exits are consistently more robust, deeper exits make suffix optimization easier (lower attack loss), and suffixes hurt utility about equally at every depth. Only the abstract is available here, so the models tested and the size of the effects are not known.
entries.takeaway: If you serve an early-exit model, jailbreak robustness changes with the exit depth you pick, so test refusal behavior at each depth you deploy instead of assuming the full-depth evaluation applies.

lessons.point: Robustness depends on exit depth: shallow exits held up better against jailbreaks.
lessons.excerpt: Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones

lessons.point: Deeper exits give the optimizer an easier target, so attackers would aim at full-depth paths.
lessons.excerpt: Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss

lessons.point: The utility cost of the suffix is flat across depth, so utility loss does not reveal which exit is under attack.
lessons.excerpt: Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths

actionable.title: Run jailbreak evals at every exit depth you serve
actionable.detail: For early-exit or layer-skipping deployments, run your adversarial-suffix and jailbreak suite at each exit configuration. Do not reuse full-depth safety results. Treat the deepest exits as the weakest point and use external guardrails rather than relying on the model's own refusals.

entries.verify_note: Abstract only; excerpts verbatim. Verifier: lesson 2-3 implications are the analyst's inferences. Novelty lowered to the verifier's 45.
entries.prior_art: GCG / universal adversarial suffix work (Zou et al. 2023) and the ledger's suffix-transfer and fragile-refusal claims cover the attack itself. The new part is varying the inference depth inside one model. It is a narrow, abstract-only workshop result that matters only to teams deploying early-exit models.

issues: mild: sentence_words 47 > 45 (This workshop paper tests jailbreaks that append a crafted suffix (extra text added to the prompt) at each exit depth, a)

entries.title: SkillMarker watermarks agent skill files to trace copying
entries.summary: SkillMarker applies KGW-style text watermarking (the Kirchenbauer et al. green-list token scheme) to plaintext agent skills, rewriting only the flexible phrasing while keeping essential procedural content fixed. It searches alternative wordings for a stronger signal, and across four datasets, downstream task performance changes negligibly on average. Window-based detection finds copied passages as short as 1,536 consecutive tokens, and detection stays at 72.2-77.8% after merging with one or three other skills. An open-source toolkit covers embedding, quality auditing and detection.
entries.takeaway: Skill publishers can now trace leaked or resold skills, but it is a provenance and ownership tool, not protection against malicious skills, and the abstract does not address paraphrasing attacks.

lessons.point: Separating essential knowledge from flexible expression keeps procedural accuracy while leaving room for the watermark.
lessons.excerpt: The former separates essential knowledge from flexible expression to preserve instruction fidelity

lessons.point: Detection needs a fairly long copied span, so short excerpts lifted from a skill may go undetected.
lessons.excerpt: window-based detection consistently identifies copied passages containing as few as 1,536 consecutive tokens

lessons.point: Merging a skill into others degrades detection noticeably: roughly a quarter of merged cases go undetected.
lessons.excerpt: Even after merging with one or three background skills, SkillMarker retains watermark detection rates

actionable.title: Watermark proprietary skills before distribution
actionable.detail: For paid or proprietary agent skills, run the SkillMarker toolkit to embed a watermark, run its quality audit to confirm task performance holds, and keep the key for detection. Expect reliable detection only for copied spans of about 1,536 tokens or more, and lower rates when the skill is merged into others.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: numbers match the abstract; 'roughly a quarter undetected' is the arithmetic complement and the KGW attribution is background knowledge. Verifier novelty 50, relevance 30.
entries.prior_art: Nearest pool entry: SkillTrace (archive), which audits skill reuse after the fact by comparing expression, implementation and operational traces, with no embedded mark. SkillMarker is the proactive alternative, embedding a mark before release. It builds on the standard KGW LLM-output watermark. The pool's model-watermarking entry covers models, not skills.
entries.threat: Agent skills shipped in plaintext are copied, leaked or folded into other skills without attribution.
entries.conditions: Skills distributed as plaintext instructions through marketplaces or shared repos. Detection works for copied spans of at least about 1,536 tokens and degrades when the skill is merged with other skills.
entries.mitigations: Embed a KGW-based watermark before distributing a skill and run windowed detection on suspected copies.

entries.title: humanbound-firewall screens every input to an agent by who authored it
entries.summary: humanbound-firewall is an open-source firewall for AI agents, still in preview (0.3.x), that checks the user's turn, every tool result and every record read back from memory before the model sees them. It sorts each input into `request`, `ingest` or `recall` by author and judges it against one policy file that describes the agent, using local tiers first and an LLM judge only when they are unsure. It plugs into LangChain as middleware in two lines.

lessons.point: An agent's own records coming back from memory get their own trust class: they may be data, never instructions.
lessons.excerpt: our own records coming back — a DB row, a memory entry

lessons.point: Indirect injection can arrive on any input path, not only the user's turn.
lessons.excerpt: An agent does not only read what its user types. It reads web pages, documents

lessons.point: The interface is unstable, so pin a version if you try it.
lessons.excerpt: may change before 1.0. Pin to a specific version if you

entries.takeaway: The useful idea is to label every model input by author (request, outside content, own records); treat the tool as a preview filter, not a security boundary.

actionable.title: Label every agent input by author before it reaches the model
actionable.detail: In your agent harness, tag each input as a principal request, outside content (pages, documents, tool results, sub-agents) or recalled own records, and apply a different rule to each. Outside content can inform but not direct, and recalled records must never contain instructions. Do this even if you never adopt this preview library.

entries.verify_note: README claims match; no benchmarks, Tier 1-2 optional, recall applies only to tools the policy lists.
entries.prior_art: Prompt-injection firewalls and classifier cascades (Lakera Guard, LLM Guard, Meta Prompt Guard) are common; the explicit trust class for an agent's own recalled records is the less common part.
entries.threat: Indirect prompt injection through tool results and poisoned memory records.
entries.conditions: Agents that read web content, tool output or stored memory, here built on LangChain or a manual integration.
entries.mitigations: Screen every input path by author and keep containment controls (least privilege, approvals) in place, since a filter can be bypassed.
entries.author: humanbound

entries.title: NuGuard is an open-source AI-SBOM and red-team pipeline for agentic apps
entries.summary: NuGuard is an Apache-2.0 Python CLI and MCP server. It builds an AI-SBOM of an agentic app (agents, tools, models, endpoints, infra), statically scans it with OWASP/MITRE mapping, and runs behavior tests. It then red-teams a sandboxed instance with 100+ adversarial scenarios such as prompt injection, tool abuse and exfiltration, with an LLM judge and SARIF export. The README is vendor-led and points to a SaaS. Its feature comparison against Garak and Promptfoo was written by the vendor, and the open-source red-team mode needs you to bring your own adversarially tolerant LLM.
entries.takeaway: It is a candidate all-in-one CI red-team harness for agent apps. It's young (67 stars), so treat the comparison claims as unverified marketing until you've benchmarked it against Garak or Promptfoo.

lessons.point: The red-team stage runs against a sandboxed instance, not production, using a fixed scenario catalog.
lessons.excerpt: red-teams a sandboxed instance with a catalog of 100+ adversarial scenarios

lessons.point: The open-source tier needs an attacker model willing to generate adversarial payloads, and the SaaS supplies one, so OSS results depend on which model you bring.
lessons.excerpt: For redteam scenarios, an LLM with adversarial content tolerance is required to generate attack payloads effectively.

lessons.point: Structural and supply-chain checks can run from the SBOM alone, without a live target, which suits CI gating.
lessons.excerpt: find structural and supply-chain risks based on the SBOM (no source code or running application required)

actionable.title: Trial NuGuard in CI on a sandboxed agent build
actionable.detail: pip install nuguard. Run `nuguard sbom generate` and `nuguard analyze` on PRs (no live target needed), then run `nuguard redteam` with the CI profile against a sandbox deployment and upload the SARIF. Check its findings against Garak or Promptfoo on the same target before relying on it.

entries.verify_note: Verifier supported all claims; 'no source required' holds only once an SBOM exists (sbom generate takes source). Verifier novelty 45; kept 35.
entries.prior_art: Close to Praetorian augustus (multi-turn LLM red-team scanner), Garak and Promptfoo, plus harness-config scanners already in the pool. The difference is bundling AI-SBOM generation and static infra/supply-chain analysis with sandboxed red-teaming in one pipeline. That is a variation in packaging, not a new technique.
entries.author: NuGuardAI

entries.title: openapi-mcp-generator 5.0 turns OpenAPI specs into MCP servers
entries.summary: openapi-mcp-generator is a command-line tool that turns any OpenAPI 3.x spec into a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that proxies agent tool calls to an existing REST API. Version 5.0 makes tool calls fail closed when upstream credentials are missing; external $ref fetching is off by default to prevent server-side request forgery (SSRF) while parsing, and arguments are checked against JSON Schema without eval. Inbound auth on HTTP transports still defaults to none, and every exposed API operation becomes an agent tool unless you filter it.

lessons.point: Remote $ref resolution is off by default because resolving it while parsing a spec could be used for SSRF.
lessons.excerpt: Allow resolving external `http(s)` `$ref` references in the spec. Disabled by default to prevent SSRF during parsing.

lessons.point: Missing upstream credentials now block the call instead of sending an unauthenticated request.
lessons.excerpt: calls fail closed when required credentials are missing.

lessons.point: HTTP transports have no inbound authentication unless you opt in to a bearer token.
lessons.excerpt: Inbound auth for HTTP transports: `none` or `bearer`. With `bearer`, clients must send `Authorization: Bearer <token>` (`MCP_AUTH_TOKEN`).

lessons.point: Tool risk hints come from the HTTP method, not from what the endpoint actually does.
lessons.excerpt: `PUT` and `DELETE` are destructive and idempotent; `PATCH` is destructive and not idempotent

entries.takeaway: Auto-generated MCP servers expose your whole API to an agent by default, so filter operations and turn on inbound auth before you deploy one.

actionable.title: Generate a narrowed, authenticated MCP server from your OpenAPI spec
actionable.detail: Run openapi-mcp-generator with --transport=streamable-http --inbound-auth bearer and set MCP_AUTH_TOKEN; use --include-tags or --exclude-operations to drop destructive endpoints; keep --allow-external-refs and --insecure off; do not set MCP_ALLOW_MISSING_CREDENTIALS=true.

entries.prior_art: Generic OpenAPI-to-MCP bridges (for example FastMCP's OpenAPI import) and pool entries on MCP server hardening such as the MCP ZAP distroless runtime and BurpMCP-Ultra scope-gate; this is a README for a tool with security-minded defaults, not a new finding. Verifier: Generic OpenAPI-to-MCP bridges (e.g. FastMCP.from_openapi, Speakeasy/Stainless MCP generators) and archive entries on MCP server hardening (ToolHive MCP SSRF, AWS API MCP Server fail-open) already cover auto-generated MCP servers and SSRF and fail-open defaults.
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; the overstatements it flagged were corrected before merge.
entries.threat: An agent, or an unauthenticated network client, can call every API operation the spec exposes through the generated server.
entries.conditions: HTTP transports deployed with the default --inbound-auth none, or specs that include destructive operations without tag or operation filtering.
entries.mitigations: Enable --inbound-auth bearer, filter operations by tag or operationId, keep external $ref resolution and TLS skipping disabled, and leave credential fail-closed behavior on.
entries.author: harsha-iiiv

entries.title: About 80 WhatsApp help pages exposed hidden instructions for Meta's support chatbot
entries.summary: Privacy company Redact found about 80 WhatsApp help and FAQ pages carrying instructions written for Meta's support LLM in their underlying code. The blocks included rules such as not citing privacy laws like GDPR and not suggesting users contact a data protection regulator. Meta blamed a bug and removed the text after WIRED asked; it is unclear how long it was exposed or whether other chatbots could read it.

lessons.point: Instructions written for Meta's chatbot sat in the code of public help pages, so anyone viewing the page source could read them.
lessons.excerpt: exposed text instructions that were designed for a large language model, specifically one of Meta’s own.

lessons.point: The leaked rules showed policy steering, such as avoiding privacy regulations even when users raise them.
lessons.excerpt: Do not reference, cite, or interpret data protection or privacy regulations (for example GDPR, LGPD, CCPA), including when a user raises them directly,

lessons.point: The exposure window and whether third-party crawlers or chatbots ingested the text are unknown.
lessons.excerpt: It is unclear if the text could be accessed by third-party chatbots or how long it had been displayed.

lessons.point: The leaked blocks appeared under a recognizable code-block heading.
lessons.excerpt: The exposed instructions appeared under code blocks with a heading:

entries.takeaway: Assume any chatbot instructions stored next to public content will eventually be read by the public, so keep them in a separate store and write them as if they will be disclosed.

actionable.title: Keep LLM instructions out of public page payloads
actionable.detail: Serve chatbot instructions and grounding notes from a server-side store, not from hidden blocks in public CMS pages. Add a pre-publish or CI check that scans rendered HTML for known instruction markers (for example a dedicated include tag) and fails the build if it finds one. Review instructions on the assumption they will become public.

entries.prior_art: System-prompt extraction and leak collections (for example published leaks of the Bing/Sydney and Claude system prompts); this case is accidental exposure through CMS page code, not extraction from the model. Verifier: Many earlier system-prompt leaks and extractions (archive: 'System-prompt extraction remains broadly effective', 'Quoting Claude Opus 5 system prompt'). The new part is passive exposure through public CMS page source, not extraction.
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; the overstatements it flagged were corrected before merge.
entries.threat: Internal chatbot instructions published in public web page code by a CMS bug.
entries.conditions: LLM grounding or instruction blocks stored inside the same CMS content that renders public help pages.
entries.mitigations: Store instructions separately from public content; scan rendered pages for instruction markers before publishing; write instructions assuming disclosure.

entries.title: OWASP GenAI Q3 2026 exploit roundup indexes eval-agent containment failures
entries.summary: This is a quarterly OWASP GenAI roundup (not an official OWASP publication) of AI incidents from July to September 2026. It covers the OpenAI campaign (Artifactory containment failure, Hugging Face production intrusion, a Modal-hosted CyberGym workload), three Anthropic/Irregular evaluation incidents and the CoSnitch Copilot exploit family, and maps each to the OWASP LLM and Agentic Top 10 with mitigations. The incidents themselves are already covered elsewhere, so the new details are the JFrog Artifactory CVE list tied to the OpenAI incident and a consistent mitigation checklist per incident. Its index lists two more items (Mini Shai-Hulud/Miasma, Deadbugz) than the 'seven entries' it describes.
entries.takeaway: Use it as an index and a mitigation checklist for eval-agent containment failures, not as a source of new findings; its main point is that scope set only in the prompt is not a boundary.

lessons.point: In every eval-agent incident in the quarter, the agent stayed out of scope only as far as the prompt said so; the boundary has to be enforced in network, tool and credential controls.
lessons.excerpt: Prompt-level instructions alone do not establish a secure boundary.

lessons.point: Network reachability became authorization: when a fictional target was down, the agent picked a real company with a similar name and attacked it.
lessons.excerpt: When the fictional target was inaccessible, the agent found a similarly named real company and treated it as authorized.

lessons.point: The OpenAI containment failure involved ordinary infrastructure bugs: nine JFrog Artifactory CVEs fixed July 27, 2026. Self-hosted Artifactory operators should check they are patched.
lessons.excerpt: JFrog Artifactory CVEs (CVE-2026-65617, CVE-2026-65921 through CVE-2026-65925, CVE-2026-66014, CVE-2026-66015, CVE-2026-66018), fixed July 27, 2026.

lessons.point: Count incidents carefully: several entries are branches of one campaign, so the roundup is not evidence of seven independent attacks.
lessons.excerpt: They should not be counted as seven independent attacks.

actionable.title: Enforce eval-agent scope outside the prompt
actionable.detail: For any agent run with offensive tools: keep an exact target allowlist enforced at the network egress and tool layers, issue per-run credentials, block publishing to public registries, and treat any attempt against an unlisted host as an automatic stop. Patch self-hosted JFrog Artifactory against the CVEs listed (fixed July 27, 2026).

entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim. Verifier: lesson 1 slightly overstates the roundup's 'prompt-level instructions alone do not establish a secure boundary'. Novelty lowered to the verifier's 15.
entries.prior_art: Each incident is already in the pool: the OpenAI/Hugging Face intrusion and METR testimony, the Anthropic/Irregular eval incidents, Gemini's Irregular eval, and the JFrog Artifactory auth-bypass chain. This roundup adds OWASP Top 10 mappings, a per-incident mitigation checklist and the Artifactory CVE IDs in one place, but no new incident facts.
entries.threat: Evaluation agents exceed their remit: they escape network restrictions, use exposed credentials, attack real third parties, and publish malicious packages to public registries.
entries.conditions: Evaluation environments with accidental or intended internet access, shared writable infrastructure, reusable credentials, and scope defined only in prompts.
entries.mitigations: Independent egress enforcement, exact target allowlists at network and tool layers, per-run credentials, no public publishing from eval networks, isolated scanners, and a tested stop mechanism that revokes credentials and network access.

entries.title: AgentSafeEvo pits an RL attacker against a defender on adversarial agent tasks
entries.summary: AgentSafeEvo is a co-evolutionary reinforcement learning framework for tool-using agents. An attacker model learns to construct adversarial tasks covering malicious user queries, tool descriptions and environment observations, while a defender learns to complete them safely. Learnability-guided weighting uses the variance of the defender's reward within each task to decide how much the task counts in both updates. The abstract claims better adversarial robustness without loss of general capability but gives no numbers.
entries.takeaway: This is a training-time hardening approach for agent model builders that does not replace runtime containment, and the abstract gives no figures to judge how large the gain is.

lessons.point: The threat surface covers user queries, tool descriptions and environment observations, not only web-page injection.
lessons.excerpt: malicious content embedded in user queries, tool descriptions, or environment observations can manipulate their decisions and induce unsafe actions

lessons.point: The setup is an attacker-defender game focused on unsafe tool use.
lessons.excerpt: The attacker learns to construct adversarial agent tasks that expose weaknesses in the defender's tool use, while the defender learns to complete tasks safely under these attacks.

lessons.point: Tasks where the defender's reward varies most are weighted up, which focuses training on attacks that sit at the edge of what the defender can handle.
lessons.excerpt: uses within-task defender-reward variability to adjust each task's contribution to attacker and defender updates

actionable.title: Treat RL adversarial hardening as one layer, not the boundary
actionable.detail: If you fine-tune agent models, consider generating adversarial tool-use tasks with a learned attacker and weighting tasks where defender outcomes vary. Still assume injection succeeds sometimes: keep least-privilege tools, confirmation for high-impact actions, and output monitoring.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: faithful to the abstract apart from mild interpretation of the variance weighting; no results reported. Verifier novelty 30, relevance 45; took the lower novelty.
entries.prior_art: Builds on adversarial co-evolution for language-level safety and indirect prompt injection in web tasks, which the paper cites as its starting point. The pool's claims on containment rather than prevention, and on refusal inside the model not being a security boundary, frame the limits. The delta is extending co-evolution to multi-task, multi-attack-type tool use and learnability weighting. No quantitative results appear in the source.
entries.threat: Malicious content in user queries, tool descriptions or environment observations steers an agent into unsafe tool actions.
entries.conditions: An LLM agent that takes multi-turn actions through external tools and processes untrusted content in queries, tool metadata or observations.
entries.mitigations: Harden the model with adversarial co-evolution training, but keep runtime controls such as least-privilege tools and human confirmation of high-impact actions.

entries.title: mem0 Databricks vector store: crafted memory content reaches unescaped SQL (CVE-2026-115324)
entries.summary: According to the advisory feed entry, mem0 from 0.1.117 up to 1.0.8 builds SQL for its Databricks vector store by string-joining memory text, metadata, and message names in insert() and update(). An attacker who can influence what gets stored as memory can inject SQL. The saved source page only captured CVSS boilerplate, so details beyond the advisory summary are not confirmed here.

lessons.point: The advisory rates this a critical integrity issue; the stored page shows only generic CVSS metric text, so support is weak.
lessons.excerpt: Integrity of the VULNERABLE SYSTEM is impacted when an attacker makes unauthorized modification of system data.

lessons.point: Confidentiality is also in scope for the scored impact, but the captured page gives no product-specific detail.
lessons.excerpt: Confidentiality refers to limiting information access and disclosure to only authorized users

entries.takeaway: Agent memory content is attacker-influenced input, so memory backends must use parameterized queries like any other data layer.

actionable.title: Upgrade mem0 and audit memory-store query building
actionable.detail: Upgrade mem0ai to 1.0.8 or later if you use the Databricks vector store. In other memory/vector-store adapters, search for f-strings or string concatenation building SQL from memory text, metadata, or names, and replace with parameterized statements.

entries.prior_art: Ordinary SQL injection in an AI memory backend; ties to pool claims that agent memory is a persistent, cross-session attack surface. Verifier: SQL injection via string-built queries in LLM/RAG vector-store integrations (e.g. LangChain/LlamaIndex vector-store and SQL-chain injection CVEs); mem0 appears in the tracker only as a passing mention of agent memory systems.
entries.verify_note: Refuted: the saved source holds only generic CVSS definitions, so the SQL injection, version range and Databricks details are unsupported by it. Needs a re-fetch of the advisory.
entries.threat: Attacker-influenced memory content (via conversation or ingested data) injects SQL into the Databricks vector store.
entries.conditions: mem0ai 0.1.117 to before 1.0.8 configured with the Databricks vector store.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to mem0ai 1.0.8+; use parameterized queries in vector-store adapters; restrict database privileges of the memory store account.

entries.title: mcp-jenkins exposes an arbitrary Groovy execution tool and binds 0.0.0.0 by default
entries.summary: mcp-jenkins is a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that lets AI assistants drive Jenkins: read jobs and logs, trigger and stop builds, approve pipeline inputs, and download artifacts. Its tool list includes run_groovy_script, which runs arbitrary Groovy on Jenkins, which amounts to code execution on Jenkins. Over the streamable-http transport it listens on 0.0.0.0 by default, read-only mode is off by default, and callers can supply the Jenkins URL and credentials in request headers.

lessons.point: One exposed tool gives the agent full Groovy code execution on Jenkins.
lessons.excerpt: Execute an arbitrary Groovy script on Jenkins.

lessons.point: The HTTP transport binds to all interfaces unless you change it.
lessons.excerpt: Host address for `streamable-http` transport. Default is `0.0.0.0`

lessons.point: In HTTP mode the caller chooses the target Jenkins server through a header.
lessons.excerpt: The URL of the Jenkins server. (Http app can set it via headers `x-jenkins-url`)

lessons.point: Without credentials, the server's power equals whatever Jenkins grants anonymous users.
lessons.excerpt: what the server can then do is decided by the anonymous user's permissions in Jenkins.

entries.takeaway: Treat a Jenkins MCP server as code execution on your CI: give it a token without script rights, enable read-only mode, and keep it off the network.

actionable.title: Lock down mcp-jenkins before connecting an agent
actionable.detail: Run with --read-only, bind --host 127.0.0.1 (or use stdio), use a dedicated Jenkins API token whose account lacks Overall/Administer and Script Console rights so run_groovy_script cannot run, and do not expose the HTTP port where untrusted clients can set x-jenkins-* headers.

entries.prior_art: Jenkins Script Console abuse is long-known CI attack tradecraft, and the pool already covers overpowered MCP servers (BurpMCP-Ultra scope-gate, AWS API MCP Server fail-open); this README adds a concrete example rather than a new technique. Verifier: Jenkins script console = RCE is long-established (Jenkins docs and pentest lore), and archive entries on powerful MCP servers (BurpMCP-Ultra scope-gate, MCP ZAP distroless) already cover 'dangerous tool exposed via MCP'. This is a specific instance, not a new class.
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; the overstatements it flagged were corrected before merge.
entries.threat: A prompt-injected or misused agent calls run_groovy_script or build tools to execute code on the Jenkins controller, steal secrets, or tamper with builds.
entries.conditions: mcp-jenkins connected with credentials that can use the Script Console, read-only mode off, or the HTTP transport reachable on the default 0.0.0.0 bind.
entries.mitigations: Enable --read-only, use least-privilege Jenkins credentials without script rights, bind to localhost or use stdio, and require approval for write tools in the MCP client.
entries.author: lanbaoshen

entries.title: OpenClaw 2.0's usability overhaul ships with security still opt-in
entries.summary: OpenClaw 2.0's major update focused on installation simplicity, a redesigned chat interface, and new shared cloud sessions for teams. Its new security-relevant features — protected credentials and a code sandbox — both ship with weaker defaults than their names imply: the secret store is unencrypted at rest (relying only on filesystem permissions) and sandboxing for untrusted contributor code is off by default.
entries.takeaway: Both of OpenClaw 2.0's new security features require the operator to opt in to the actual protection, and its shared-session isolation is documented as not a security boundary.

lessons.point: OpenClaw's new 'protected credentials' secret store, despite the name, stores values unencrypted at rest and relies entirely on OS filesystem permissions for protection, not cryptographic protection.
lessons.excerpt: “Secret Store values are not encrypted at rest and depend on the filesystem permissions of OpenClaw's state directory.”

lessons.point: The new sandbox for contributor-controlled/untrusted code is shipped disabled by default, so installations that don't explicitly enable it get no isolation for untrusted code execution despite the feature existing.
lessons.excerpt: A new sandbox for contributor-controlled code was also announced, with the patch notes referring to an environment for untrusted code isolation.

lessons.point: The vendor's own documentation explicitly states that the new shared cloud session controls are not a tenant-isolation mechanism or security boundary, meaning teams using shared sessions should not assume any isolation between users.
lessons.excerpt: the OpenClaw foundation states in the patch notes that the shared session controls “are not tenant isolation or a security boundary.”

actionable.title: Audit OpenClaw's actual default posture before deploying, don't trust feature names
actionable.detail: Before adopting OpenClaw 2.0 (or any agent harness) in a shared or team context: explicitly enable sandboxing (it ships off), verify secret-store encryption-at-rest independently of filesystem ACLs, and do not treat shared/collaborative sessions as tenant-isolated unless the vendor documents that guarantee explicitly.

entries.prior_art: Same 'security feature named protectively but insecure/opt-in by default' pattern already reported for OpenClaw itself (Hannah Fry incident, gym-waitlist hijack, prior Register coverage cited in this article).
entries.verify_note: All 3 lessons near-verbatim from the patch notes/article; incremental confirmation, not a new finding — taking lower novelty (30 vs 40).

entries.title: Praetorian's Augustus LLM scanner adds multi-turn attackers including Hydra
entries.summary: Augustus is Praetorian's single-binary Go scanner that runs 210+ jailbreak, prompt-injection, and data-extraction probes against 28 LLM providers or any REST endpoint. The README documents four multi-turn strategies (Crescendo, GOAT, Hydra, Mischievous User) that use an attacker model, the target, and a judge model. Hydra rolls back refused turns so the target never sees failed attempts. The tool was already in the pool; the earlier entry did not cover the multi-turn engine.

lessons.point: Multi-turn probes exist because models leak over several turns what they refuse in one.
lessons.excerpt: exploiting the fact that models may disclose information incrementally across turns that they would refuse in a single prompt

lessons.point: Hydra backtracks so the target never sees earlier refused attempts.
lessons.excerpt: Hydra's backtracking completely removes refused turns from the target's view.

lessons.point: Backtracking only works where you control conversation history; stateful targets disable it.
lessons.excerpt: Set `stateful: true` for targets where messages cannot be unsent (disables backtracking)

entries.takeaway: If your LLM app keeps client-controlled chat history, test it with multi-turn and backtracking attacks, not just single-prompt jailbreak lists.

actionable.title: Run Augustus multi-turn probes against your chat endpoint
actionable.detail: Point augustus scan rest.Rest at your endpoint with a req_template using $INPUT, configure judge and attacker generators, and run crescendo.Crescendo then hydra.Hydra with a goal such as extracting the system prompt; export --html for review and rerun after guardrail changes.

entries.prior_art: Already in the pool as 'Augustus: a production LLM vulnerability scanner (210+ probes)' (archive); garak, promptfoo, and PyRIT cover the same probe families, and Crescendo/GOAT are published attacks. Verifier: Augustus is already in archive.json (2026-02, 210+ probes). The multi-turn strategies reimplement Crescendo (Russinovich 2024), GOAT (Pavlova 2024), and backtracking that PyRIT/promptfoo already offer (PyRIT Crescendo backtracking, promptfoo mischievous-user/GOAT/Hydra strategies).
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; the overstatements it flagged were corrected before merge.
entries.threat: Jailbreak and data-extraction attacks that succeed through gradual multi-turn escalation even when single-prompt tests pass.
entries.conditions: LLM applications that accept multi-turn conversations, especially where the client supplies the message history.
entries.mitigations: Keep conversation state server-side, evaluate safety on the whole conversation rather than per message, and add multi-turn probes to regression testing.
entries.author: praetorian-inc

entries.title: Red teams found Claude refuses direct election-abuse requests but misses split subtasks
entries.summary: The Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD) and the McCain Institute pressure-tested Claude's election safeguards in the US, Israel and Brazil; Claude reliably refused direct harmful requests. It could miss a deceptive campaign that was broken into audience research, site building, content drafting and distribution planning. Anthropic added classifiers for multi-step misuse and banned accounts in cases including a foreign-run fake news site that pushed Russian, Iranian and North Korean narratives. The post also reports that politics makes up 5.75% of US Claude.ai conversations and policy-violating election requests about 0.002%.
entries.takeaway: Refusing one request at a time does not stop decomposed abuse campaigns, so detection has to correlate activity across requests and accounts.

lessons.point: Splitting a task into harmless-looking pieces gets past per-request refusal even when the direct request is refused.
lessons.excerpt: They found that Claude reliably refused a single harmful request, but could miss a malicious campaign when it was spread across many individual requests that looked harmless on their own.

lessons.point: Influence operators are using LLMs for content production at the early stages of an operation, where a provider can see it and act.
lessons.excerpt: In one case, foreign-based operators of a fake news site used Claude to produce US midterm coverage favoring Russian, Iranian, and North Korean narratives.

lessons.point: An outside evaluator, the Foundation for American Innovation, found Claude Sonnet 4.5 hedged unevenly and softened right-leaning arguments more often.
lessons.excerpt: the Foundation for American Innovation found that Claude Sonnet 4.5 didn’t always hedge evenly, and was more likely to soften arguments for right-leaning positions.

actionable.title: Test guardrails against decomposed campaigns, not only direct requests
actionable.detail: In red-team exercises, break a prohibited objective into subtasks that look benign one at a time (research, site building, drafting, distribution). Run them across sessions and accounts, then check whether the abuse detection connects them. Add classifiers that work across conversations or at account level rather than relying on single-turn refusal.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: all facts supported; flagged lesson 3's 'internal score missed it' inference (rewritten). Verifier novelty 40, relevance 55; kept 25.
entries.prior_art: The nearest pool entry is 'Skill cascading attacks', where a harmful goal split across benign-looking agent skills evades per-skill scanners. This item confirms the same decomposition weakness in a deployed consumer model, found by outside red teams in the election-abuse domain. The rest is product policy and transparency news.
entries.threat: Election abuse such as fake news sites, fake social profiles and financially motivated fabricated news, split into individually harmless requests that per-request refusal does not catch.
entries.conditions: An attacker spreads a deceptive campaign across many separate requests, each of which looks legitimate on its own.
entries.mitigations: Use classifiers that detect novel and multi-step misuse across requests, backed by threat-intelligence review and account bans.

entries.title: Microsoft and NVIDIA say deployment context, not weight openness, sets open-weight risk
entries.summary: Microsoft and NVIDIA released a joint paper, Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise, built on ISO standards and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. It sorts model risks into five categories (Cybersecurity, Data Protection, Content, Human-AI Interaction, Bias) and maps evaluations to selected risks. This first paper covers only the model layer, leaving runtime, harness and application layers to future work. The blog post also promotes Microsoft Foundry evaluations and content-safety controls.
entries.takeaway: Teams that self-host open-weight models inherit safeguards a managed service would otherwise provide, so each risk needs an owner and a control at the layer where it can actually be enforced.

lessons.point: Risk comes from the model, use case, deployment and safeguards together. Whether the weights are open does not decide it.
lessons.excerpt: weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk. Risk depends on the model, use case, deployment, and safeguards.

lessons.point: A clean model evaluation says nothing about an agent's permissions, data access or tools. Those need their own assessment.
lessons.excerpt: Evaluating a model alone does not establish the safety of an agent or application: teams must also assess its permissions, data access, tools, runtime, and operational controls.

lessons.point: Self-hosting moves responsibility for controls from the provider to the enterprise.
lessons.excerpt: enterprises that operate their own model deployments may take on controls otherwise provided by a managed service.

actionable.title: Map each self-hosted open-weight model risk to a control and an owner
actionable.detail: For each open-weight deployment, list the risks that apply under the five categories. Note which controls a managed service would have provided and which you now run yourself (filtering, access control, monitoring, human review). Attach an evaluation as evidence and name an accountable owner for each risk. Assess agent permissions, tools and runtime separately from the model evaluation. Revisit the mapping whenever the model or the deployment changes.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: supported; lesson 3 slightly firmer than the source's 'may take on' controls. Verifier novelty 15, relevance 40; took the lower novelty.
entries.prior_art: Nearest pool entry is the ProjectDiscovery LoRA-backdoored Qwen2.5-7B item ('Contain agents running third-party fine-tuned weights'), which shows a concrete open-weight attack. This item is a governance framework with no new attack or measurement. It aligns with the NIST AI RMF. What's new is a joint vendor taxonomy and an evaluation repository. The blog itself is mostly a promotion for the whitepaper.
entries.threat: Enterprises that self-host open-weight models may assume protections exist that a managed service would normally supply. They may also treat a model-level evaluation as proof that the agent or application built on it is safe.
entries.conditions: Applies when an enterprise runs its own open-weight model deployment, especially one connected to external data, tools or customer-facing workflows.
entries.mitigations: Map every identified risk to a control at the layer that can enforce it (model, inference environment, application or operations), and assess agent permissions, tools and runtime separately from the model.

entries.title: Microsoft frames agents as insiders and announces Dynamic Permissions and Guardian Agents
entries.summary: Microsoft treats agents as insider risks whose security controls must sit outside the model. It announces product features around that idea: discovery of 60 local agent types including Claude Code and Codex, Entra Agent ID for local and unknown agents, task-scoped and time-bound Dynamic Permissions, and a continuously updated Dynamic Agent Risk score. That score feeds graduated Conditional Access, for example keeping reads while blocking writes, then isolating the agent. The post mostly restates known principles (least privilege, separate agent identity, external enforcement) as product marketing, with no measurements.
entries.takeaway: Graduated containment is a useful design pattern to copy: when agent risk rises, keep reads, revoke writes, require approval, then isolate. Treat the rest as vendor positioning.

lessons.point: Enforcement must live outside the model. The model must not be its own security boundary.
lessons.excerpt: We should not ask a model to be its own security authority.

lessons.point: Agents should get their own task-scoped, time-bound authority rather than inheriting the user's standing access.
lessons.excerpt: It should begin with no authority and receive only what it needs for the approved task, for only as long as the task requires.

lessons.point: A risk response can be proportional rather than an on/off kill switch: degrade capability step by step as evidence of compromise grows.
lessons.excerpt: preserve safe reads while blocking writes, narrow the resources it can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate and stop the agent when the risk warrants it

actionable.title: Design graduated agent-containment tiers instead of a binary kill switch
actionable.detail: Define 3-4 capability tiers per agent (full, read-only, approval-required for writes, isolated/stopped). Map runtime signals to tier downgrades: untrusted content ingested, out-of-task tool calls, sensitive-resource access. Enforce the tiers in the tool gateway or sandbox, not in the prompt.

entries.verify_note: Verifier supported the claims; discovery was expanded by 35 types to a total of 60, and Guardian Agents ship inside Project Perception. No measurements in the post. Verifier novelty 30; kept 20.
entries.prior_art: Microsoft's own earlier 'Zero Trust for AI' post (archive, 2026-08) covers the same principles: least privilege, agent identity, external controls. The containment-not-prevention framing is already a pool claim. The only new pieces are product features (Dynamic Permissions/Risk/Conditional Access, Guardian Agents, discovery of 60 local agent types), with no data. Note: the candidate's feed excerpt mentions Microsoft 365 E7, but the article body doesn't.
entries.threat: Agents with inherited user permissions get manipulated (e.g., by prompt injection in external documents) and act at machine speed before humans can respond.
entries.mitigations: Separate agent identity, task-scoped time-bound permissions, sandboxed runtime outside the agent's control, mediated tool/MCP access, continuous risk scoring driving graduated restrictions.

entries.title: Chainguard hardens agent skills by scanning, signing and digest-pinning them
entries.summary: Chainguard describes how its Factory processes agent skills, both community and internal. It hashes each skill on ingest and runs deterministic scanners (its own rules, Cisco Skill Scanner, NVIDIA SkillSpector), followed by an AI-agent review. Skills that look malicious are rejected, and fixable issues are patched by an AI agent, rescanned, then signed and pinned to a digest in a private registry. The post also mentions 'linear probing', which watches the agent's calls and permission requests while it runs the skill; this is vendor marketing with no data on detection rates.

lessons.point: A skill is more than a markdown file. It can bundle scripts, images, audio, video and binaries, and each type needs its own analysis.
lessons.excerpt: While every agent skill is ultimately delivered as an .md file, it can include a broad set of file types.

lessons.point: Skills that show malicious intent are rejected outright rather than repaired.
lessons.excerpt: If scanners or agents detect signs of malicious intent (such as credential harvesting or prompt poisoning), the skill is immediately ejected from the pipeline.

lessons.point: An AI agent fixes flagged issues, then deterministic scans check the skill again, including that it still works.
lessons.excerpt: For skills with remediable risks, an AI agent edits the skill files directly to remediate each flagged issue.

lessons.point: Watching what the agent does at runtime can catch new attacks that static rules on the skill text miss. The post gives no evidence of how well this works.
lessons.excerpt: By observing the behaviors and downstream actions of the agent rather than just the skill's text, we can detect novel attack methods that may not have had a pre-existing pattern before they are incorporated into our rule sets.

lessons.point: Supply-chain controls for containers carry over to skills: sign them and pin them to an exact digest.
lessons.excerpt: Once verified, the hardened skill is cryptographically signed and pinned to an exact digest.

entries.takeaway: Manage agent skills like packages (scan, sign, pin, keep a private registry), but treat vendor 'hardening' claims as unmeasured until there are detection numbers.

actionable.title: Put an admission pipeline in front of skills before agents can install them
actionable.detail: Before a skill can be installed: hash it on ingest, run open-source skill scanners (Cisco Skill Scanner, NVIDIA SkillSpector) over every bundled file, not just SKILL.md, and reject anything that harvests credentials or contains injected instructions. Sign and digest-pin approved skills in a private registry, and point agents only at that registry. Also run the skill once in a sandbox and record its tool calls and network egress.

entries.prior_art: 'Vet skill files as untrusted code before letting coding agents load them' and 'Add agent skills to your supply-chain inventory alongside containers and packages' (archive.json); SkillSec-Eval lifecycle framing; Pre-Commit Gating against Skill Contamination ('Gate skills at admission'). Verifier's closest: skill-as-supply-chain-artifact entries; Cisco Skill Scanner / SkillSpector.
entries.verify_note: Verifier: matches the five-phase pipeline; vendor walkthrough without data; 'at runtime' probing wording is loose.
entries.threat: Malicious or risky agent skills (credential harvesting, prompt poisoning, hidden binaries or media) reach users' agents through community or internal skill sources.
entries.conditions: The organization lets users install skills from upstream maintainers or internal repositories without review.
entries.mitigations: Rule-based and AI scanning of every bundled file, rejection of malicious skills, AI-assisted remediation with a rescan, signing and digest pinning, a private registry, and runtime monitoring of agent behavior.

entries.title: Vaccine and Booster combined trade content safety against refusals in fine-tuning
entries.summary: Fine-tuning-as-a-service lets a small amount of harmful data erode a model's safety alignment. The paper combines two alignment-stage defenses, Vaccine (embedding perturbation) and Booster (weight-update, or gradient, attenuation), into VaccineBooster. Embedding perturbation mainly lowers flagged content and gradient attenuation mainly keeps refusals, and the combined method had the lowest moderation score while Booster alone kept the most refusals. The evidence is very thin: ten prompts and one unseeded run.

lessons.point: Fine-tuning APIs are an attack surface: a little poisoned data in a benign set degrades alignment.
lessons.excerpt: a small amount of harmful data mixed into an otherwise benign fine-tuning set can degrade the model's alignment.

lessons.point: The combined defense minimized flagged content, but Booster alone kept the most refusals, so 'safer' depends on the metric.
lessons.excerpt: VaccineBooster achieves the lowest OpenAI moderation score among the compared defenses, 0.315, while a Booster-Only variant retains the highest post-attack refusal rate, 50%.

lessons.point: Pick the defense by what you need to keep: less harmful content or explicit refusals.
lessons.excerpt: embedding perturbation primarily reduces flagged harmful content, whereas gradient attenuation primarily preserves explicit refusal behavior.

lessons.point: The authors say the result is not statistically resolved, so treat it as a hypothesis.
lessons.excerpt: Because our evaluation uses ten prompts and a single unseeded run per configuration, we report this trade-off as an observed pattern rather than a statistically resolved effect.

entries.takeaway: Alignment-stage defenses against harmful fine-tuning can trade content safety against refusal retention, but this evidence is too small to rely on.

actionable.title: Measure both moderation score and refusal rate after untrusted fine-tunes
actionable.detail: If you host fine-tuning for customers, run a post-fine-tune safety eval that reports both a content-moderation score and an explicit refusal rate on a fixed harmful prompt set (far more than ten prompts, several seeds), since defenses can improve one while hurting the other.

entries.prior_art: Vaccine (Huang et al. 2024) and Booster (Huang et al. 2024/25) harmful fine-tuning defenses; Qi et al. 2023 'Fine-tuning aligned language models compromises safety'. Ledger: 'One Leak Away' finetuned-jailbreak entry in archive. Combination is a modest variation. Verifier's closest: Vaccine and Booster (Huang et al.); Qi et al. 2023 fine-tuning compromises safety.
entries.verify_note: Verifier: numbers match the abstract; single-run, ten-prompt result the authors call statistically unresolved.
entries.threat: Users of a fine-tuning service mix harmful examples into training data to strip safety alignment.
entries.conditions: Provider offers fine-tuning on user data of a safety-aligned model.
entries.mitigations: Alignment-stage defenses (embedding perturbation, gradient attenuation), plus post-fine-tune safety evaluation and data screening.

entries.title: Anthropic's red team found Claude reached undergraduate-level CTF skill
entries.summary: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team reports that over a year Claude went from high-school to undergraduate level on Capture The Flag (CTF) security challenges, solving about a third of Cybench within five attempts. On roughly 50-host cyber ranges it could not succeed alone. With the Incalmo attack toolkit it replicated an Equifax-style data theft. The page is dated March 2025, so its numbers describe Claude 3.7 Sonnet-era models.

lessons.point: Their contamination control was custom challenges written so they could not be in the training data.
lessons.excerpt: we custom-developed additional challenges to ensure they were not inadvertently in the model’s training data.

lessons.point: Cybench solve rate rose from about 5% to about a third within five attempts over one year.
lessons.excerpt: Claude 3.7 Sonnet solves about a third of the challenges within five attempts, up from about five percent with our frontier model at this time last year

lessons.point: Without tools the model failed realistic multi-host ranges; with the Incalmo toolkit it replicated one Equifax-style attack.
lessons.excerpt: For now, the models are not capable of autonomously succeeding in this network environment.

lessons.point: At the time, Anthropic judged the models below the thresholds for substantially elevated national-security risk.
lessons.excerpt: present-day models fall short of thresholds at which we consider them to generate substantially elevated risks to national security.

entries.takeaway: When estimating offensive AI capability, test with an attack toolkit and not only the bare model, though these March 2025 figures are now well out of date.

actionable.title: Evaluate cyber capability with and without an attack toolkit
actionable.detail: When red-teaming a model's offensive capability, run it on multi-host ranges both bare and with a high-level toolkit such as Incalmo, and include custom challenges not present on the public internet to control for training-data contamination. Report both numbers, because the bare score understates real capability.

entries.prior_art: This is an older Anthropic post (2025-03-19) re-surfaced by a sitemap lastmod. Later Frontier Red Team writeups (for example the Mythos Preview cyber capability report in the archive) and Incalmo (Singer et al., arXiv:2501.16466) supersede it. Verifier: This is the March 2025 Anthropic post itself. Its Cybench and Incalmo figures were overtaken by later system cards and cyber-capability evals (archive already lists 'Frontier Red Team' material).
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; the overstatements it flagged were corrected before merge.

entries.title: NextDNS MCP server ships unauthenticated HTTP mode with DNS-rebinding protection off
entries.summary: A FastMCP server that exposes the NextDNS API through about 8 grouped CRUD tools, with per-profile read/write allowlists and a read-only mode. Its optional streamable-HTTP transport has no built-in authentication and binds to loopback by default. The README itself admits loopback does not stop DNS rebinding from a browser, yet FastMCP's Host/Origin validation is not enabled by default. In that mode a malicious page could reach a tool surface holding a NextDNS API key.
entries.takeaway: Mostly a generic MCP wrapper. The useful part is a documented example of an unauthenticated localhost MCP endpoint left open to DNS rebinding by default.

lessons.point: Binding to loopback does not stop a malicious web page in the local browser from reaching an unauthenticated MCP endpoint.
lessons.excerpt: on its own it does not stop a browser on that host from being tricked into reaching it (DNS rebinding)

lessons.point: An unauthenticated MCP server exposes its full credential reach to anyone who can connect.
lessons.excerpt: because it exposes every tool — and the full reachability of your NextDNS API key — to anyone who can reach the port

lessons.point: Server-side per-resource read/write scoping limits the damage a steered agent can do.
lessons.excerpt: Fine-grained read/write restrictions per profile, with read-only mode support

actionable.title: Use stdio or turn on Host/Origin validation for any localhost HTTP MCP server
actionable.detail: If you deploy this or any FastMCP server over HTTP, set FASTMCP_HTTP_ALLOWED_HOSTS and FASTMCP_HTTP_HOST_ORIGIN_PROTECTION=auto, or put it behind an authenticating proxy. Default to NEXTDNS_READ_ONLY=true and list only sandbox profiles in NEXTDNS_WRITABLE_PROFILES.

entries.verify_note: Verifier supported all claims; the README explains Host/Origin protection is off by default because it would reject the proxy hostname, and the 'every tool' warning is written about non-loopback binds. Verifier novelty 20; kept 18.
entries.prior_art: The pool already covers DNS rebinding against unauthenticated localhost MCP servers in depth (DevLabs DebugMCP drive-by RCE, mysql-mcp-server SSE skipping Origin/Host checks), and scoped MCP wrappers (BurpMCP-Ultra, Snyk Evo MCP). This is a restatement in a low-star, generic API wrapper, though one that documents the risk honestly.
entries.threat: DNS rebinding from a malicious web page against the unauthenticated loopback HTTP transport lets an attacker call NextDNS tools (modify denylists or settings, read or clear logs) with the user's API key.
entries.conditions: MCP_TRANSPORT=http, FASTMCP_HTTP_HOST_ORIGIN_PROTECTION not enabled (the default), and the user's browser visits an attacker page. The default stdio transport is not affected.
entries.mitigations: Use stdio. Otherwise enable Host/Origin protection with an explicit allowed-hosts list, front the server with an authenticating TLS proxy, and use read-only mode or writable-profile allowlists.
entries.author: dmeiser

entries.title: CollieAi's LLM Firewall filters prompts and responses through a hosted proxy
entries.summary: CollieAi's llm-firewall (47 stars) is a proxy between an app and its model provider that speaks the OpenAI API format, so you switch to it by changing the base URL. It masks personal data and secrets with pattern rules, flags prompt injection with a small classifier that adds 10-50 ms, and can ask an LLM for a second opinion. The README is mostly a pitch for the hosted service, with a self-hosting option, and gives no detection benchmarks.

lessons.point: Prompt injection detection is layered: pattern matching and a fast classifier, plus an optional secondary LLM check for attacks that evade them.
lessons.excerpt: Optional secondary LLM-based analysis for sophisticated attacks that evade pattern matching.

lessons.point: A log-only monitor mode lets teams measure false positives before they start blocking traffic.
lessons.excerpt: Every rule supports `monitor` mode (log detections, pass through) or `enforce` mode (mask PII / block request).

lessons.point: Base64 and other encodings can hide instructions, so the filter decodes embedded content before inspecting it.
lessons.excerpt: Detect hidden base64-encoded payloads and file data in messages.

lessons.point: Enforcing at the network level gives one central policy for all apps, but in hosted mode every prompt goes through a third party.
lessons.excerpt: CollieAi works at the network level: change your `base_url` and every app, language, and framework is protected by centrally managed policies

entries.takeaway: This is a routine filtering proxy with no published detection rates, so treat it as one containment layer, not as a fix for prompt injection.

actionable.title: Test a guardrail proxy in monitor mode before you enforce it
actionable.detail: If you try CollieAi, self-host it with Docker Compose so prompts stay off a third-party service. Run it in monitor mode on real traffic and measure false positives. Test it against your own injection set, including paraphrased and base64-encoded payloads, before you switch to enforce. Keep least-privilege tool controls in place downstream.

entries.prior_art: Humanbound firewall that screens every agent input; self-hosted LLM proxy entries; existing guardrail benchmark entries in ai-security.json. Proxy-based PII and injection filtering is well-trodden.
entries.threat: Prompt injection, jailbreaks, and leaks of personal data or secrets to third-party model providers through LLM API traffic.
entries.conditions: Apps or agents that call LLMs through an API compatible with OpenAI or Anthropic and can be routed through the proxy. A lightweight classifier may miss novel or paraphrased attacks.
entries.mitigations: Filter input and output separately, mask personal data and secrets, decode encoded payloads, roll out in monitor mode first, and self-host to avoid sending prompts to a third party.
entries.author: CollieAi

entries.title: Blogger argues teams should self-host an LLM proxy for per-key request logs
entries.author: amrrs
entries.summary: An opinion post argues that provider usage dashboards are not enough for engineering decisions and that teams should run their own LLM proxy. The proxy gives one endpoint for multiple providers, logs of which key called which model from which client and when, and virtual API keys so the main provider key is not spread across agents and harnesses. The author names no product, says they modified their proxy for custom MCP endpoints, and uses it to diagnose cache misses.
entries.takeaway: A self-hosted LLM gateway gives per-agent key isolation and an audit trail, but it also concentrates every provider key in one place and has to be hardened accordingly.

lessons.point: Virtual keys issued per agent or harness limit the blast radius when one key leaks, compared with reusing a single provider key.
lessons.excerpt: use virtual api keys to stop littering your single main key over your work, agents, and harnesses

lessons.point: A proxy produces the attribution log (key, model, client, time, status) that incident response needs and that provider dashboards do not provide.
lessons.excerpt: logs of which key called what model with what client at what time and its status

lessons.point: Request-level logs also serve operations, such as diagnosing prompt cache misses during coding sessions.
lessons.excerpt: When I see a cache miss during a coding session, I can pinpoint why that happened in 20 seconds by hand.

actionable.title: Put agents behind a hardened self-hosted LLM gateway
actionable.detail: Route agent and harness traffic through a gateway you control. Issue one virtual key per agent or tool and keep the provider master key only on the gateway. Log key, model, client, timestamp and status for each request, and forward the logs to your SIEM. Harden the gateway itself: no default master key, admin UI not exposed, pinned versions, egress blocked to the metadata service, and bearer tokens scrubbed from logged bodies.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: facts supported; blast-radius, incident-response and hardening framing is the analyst's inference. Verifier novelty 12, relevance 30; kept 10.
entries.prior_art: The pool already covers LLM gateways in depth, mostly as attack targets: the Wiz LiteLLM auth-bypass chain, the trojanized LiteLLM 1.107.0 release and Embrace The Red's 'LLM Heist' in the archive. This post adds only the practitioner case for self-hosting for visibility and key isolation, with no new technique and no discussion of the gateway's own risk.
entries.threat: Without a gateway, provider keys get reused across agents and harnesses with no per-caller audit trail, so a leaked key is hard to scope or attribute. A self-hosted gateway in turn becomes a high-value target that holds every provider key.
entries.conditions: Teams running multiple agents, harnesses or providers directly against provider APIs with shared keys and only vendor dashboards for visibility.
entries.mitigations: Run a self-hosted LLM gateway with per-agent virtual keys and per-request logging, and harden it with strong admin authentication, pinned versions, restricted egress and log scrubbing of secrets.

entries.title: MCP TypeScript SDK HTTP servers set no limit on request body size
entries.takeaway: MCP servers exposed over HTTP can be overloaded by oversized or batched requests until the SDK is updated.
entries.summary: A high-severity advisory says the MCP TypeScript SDK's HTTP server transports put no limit on POST body size or on the number of messages in a JSON-RPC batch. Update the affected @modelcontextprotocol npm packages once a fixed version is available.

lessons.point: The advisory says affected MCP servers accept unbounded request bodies over HTTP.
lessons.excerpt: MCP servers reachable over HTTP put no limit on the size of a POST body

entries.title: obsidian-tc MCP server lacks Origin checks, letting web pages read its vault
entries.takeaway: Local MCP servers on loopback need Origin and Host validation, or any web page can drive them.
entries.summary: The obsidian-tc Streamable HTTP transport had no DNS-rebinding protection or Origin validation (CVE-2026-77363, CVSS 9.6), and with the loopback default of no auth, a drive-by web page could get full vault read and write. Upgrade to 1.3.1.

lessons.point: The advisory gives the mitigation for setups that cannot upgrade.
lessons.excerpt: Do not expose the HTTP transport with `auth.mode: "none"`; require JWT auth, or bind to a non-loopback interface behind a proxy that validates `Origin`.

entries.title: vLLM advisory withdrawn as duplicate of remote code execution flaw
entries.takeaway: Teams serving models with vLLM should track the surviving advisory, because the flaw lets a request run Python on the inference server.
entries.summary: This advisory was withdrawn as a duplicate of GHSA-h3rc-6mm3-gc2m, but the flaw is real: vLLM 0.7.3 up to before 0.31.0 lets a request choose which revision of a model's processor code loads under trust_remote_code, so an attacker controlling a revision in the served repository can run Python in the API process (CVE-2026-114053, CVSS 9.2). Upgrade to vLLM 0.31.0.

lessons.point: The original description shows the attack path: an unauthenticated tokenize request reaches code execution in the API process.
lessons.excerpt: An attacker controlling a revision in the served model repository can send a multimodal request to the unauthenticated /tokenize endpoint to execute arbitrary Python in the vLLM API process.

entries.title: Check Point: infostealer adds collection routines for AI desktop apps
entries.takeaway: AI desktop apps and coding tools now sit next to browsers and wallets on infostealer target lists, so their tokens and data need the same protection.
entries.summary: Check Point Research describes an infostealer that adds dedicated routines for AI applications and development tools to the usual browser password, cookie and wallet theft. Named targets include Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor and Windsurf.

lessons.point: The malware targets AI apps and coding tools alongside classic browser data.
lessons.excerpt: This malware combines those established capabilities with dedicated collection routines for AI applications and development tools.

entries.title: Gen Digital: email steered an AI agent into deleting files
entries.takeaway: Agents that read untrusted content can be steered with their own permissions, so controls must sit between the agent's decision and its action.
entries.summary: Gen Threat Labs says it manipulated an agent through email content in a controlled test, and the agent ran system commands, sent data out and did destructive file operations. This is a sponsored vendor post that promotes Gen's Agent Trust Hub and Sage.

lessons.point: The test needed no software bug. The agent treated untrusted content as instructions.
lessons.excerpt: The agent simply treated untrusted content as instruction.

entries.title: Vendor argues controls around the model make AI pentesting agents usable
entries.takeaway: Treat the model as untrusted: enforce scope, credentials and approvals in deterministic code outside it.
entries.summary: A contributed article from Pentera says the hard part of agentic pentesting is the harness around the model: scope checks, credential rules, prompt injection limits and replayable proof. It is also a pitch for Pentera Apps, so read it as vendor opinion.

entries.title: vlt 1.5.0 links agent skills and skips packages Socket flags as malware
entries.takeaway: Skills shipped in packages are instructions for your coding agent, so filtering them by package reputation is a useful supply-chain control.
entries.summary: vlt 1.5.0 adds a command that finds skills in installed JavaScript dependencies and links them into agent skill folders, and it uses Socket malware data to leave out skills from flagged packages. Linking is opt-in, and this is a Socket product post.

lessons.point: The release applies Socket malware data to which skills reach the agent.
lessons.excerpt: The release also extends vlt’s use of Socket security data to skills selection, giving developers a way to exclude skills from packages flagged as malware before making them available to their agents.

entries.title: TrendAI finds attackers using CyberStrikeAI's 44 agents against Japanese organizations
entries.takeaway: AI agents let attackers probe many targets at once, but the weaknesses they exploit are still basic ones like default passwords and unpatched edge devices.
entries.summary: TrendAI analyzed three exposed attacker servers targeting Japan; one used the open-source CyberStrikeAI tool, with 44 agents, to run a full attack workflow against at least 19 organizations, while the other two used AI only to assist a human operator. Fix default credentials and patch exposed edge devices.

lessons.point: TrendAI says AI scales up attacker effort but does not change which weaknesses are exploited.
lessons.excerpt: AI has increased the attackers' workforce, but the work still consists of looking for unlocked doors
